one_liner: Rust toolchain combining a formatter (97% Prettier-compatible) and linter (500+ rules) that replace ESLint and Prettier/dprint.
what_it_does: Biome is a single Rust binary that formats and lints JavaScript, TypeScript, JSX, JSON, CSS and GraphQL, replacing the separate ESLint + Prettier (or dprint) toolchain with one CLI, one config file (biome.json), and a shared LSP for editors. It ships via npm with prebuilt native binaries per platform, so the binary itself needs no Node.js runtime. `biome migrate eslint` and `biome migrate prettier` import recognized rules from existing configs, but Biome uses its own rule engine and config format rather than being a wire-compatible swap for either tool.
how_it_is_fast: It's compiled Rust, avoiding Node.js/V8 startup and interpreter overhead. Formatting and linting run against one shared lossless CST (biome_rowan, a rowan-style Green/Red tree that preserves full trivia) instead of each tool doing its own parse. Biome's own benchmark notes say the linter batches rule matching against one semantic model and control-flow graph rather than running each rule as an independent AST visitor, and the CLI parallelizes file processing across threads (tunable via the BIOME_THREADS env var). The scanner also skips filesystem traversal into folders irrelevant to the current run when project-wide type rules are disabled.
when_to_use: You already run Prettier (or dprint) + ESLint on JS/TS/JSON/CSS/GraphQL and want one faster CLI/LSP, bootstrapped from existing configs via `biome migrate`.
Editor-in-the-loop formatting/linting on medium-large monorepos where ESLint's per-keystroke latency is the pain point — Biome's LSP targets interactive use.
CI wants a fast cold full-repo check across JS/TS/CSS/GraphQL without needing type-aware rules.
You want a self-contained native binary with no Node.js dependency for the CLI itself (the npm package just wraps a platform binary).
You want broad out-of-the-box rule coverage (500+ rules pulled from ESLint/typescript-eslint/jsx-a11y/unicorn) without assembling an ESLint plugin stack.
when_not_to_use: You depend on ESLint plugins or custom rules with no Biome equivalent — `biome migrate eslint` only maps recognized rules (eslint, typescript, jsx-a11y, unicorn, jest), not arbitrary plugins.

You need full type-aware lint parity with typescript-eslint: Biome's type-aware 'project domain' rules (noFloatingPromises, noUnresolvedImports, noImportCycles) are new in v2, opt-in, and docs cite performance dropping from ~800ms to ~2s per 2,000 files when enabled.
You rely on incremental/cached formatting for large repos with few changed files — Biome has no incremental formatting like Prettier/dprint; every run is a cold run.

You want to cite the headline speedup numbers as current: the published ~25x/~15x figures are Nov 2022 Rome-era hyperfine runs, never re-measured, and the benchmark/ code that produced them was deleted from main in May 2026.

Your codebase has deeply parenthesized object expressions in arrow functions (`() => ({...})`) — a real regression made formatting 'dramatically slower' on that shape between 2.5.10 and 2.5.11 (GH #11747), a sign perf isn't uniformly stable release-to-release.

integration.form: crate (Rust workspace of 100+ biome_* crates), distributed as a prebuilt native CLI binary via the @biomejs/biome npm package
integration.dependencies: none to run (self-contained native binary; npm install only adds one platform-specific optionalDependency binary, no JS deps). Building from source needs the Rust toolchain.
integration.min_toolchain: Rust edition 2024 (~1.85+) to build from source; via npm, Node.js >=14.21.3 is only the install mechanism, not required to run the binary
integration.platforms: linux-x64/arm64 (glibc + musl), darwin-x64/arm64, win32-x64/arm64 (per npm optionalDependencies); also compiles to WASM for the online playground
integration.thread_safety: not documented in detail — the architecture docs' parallelism/daemon sections are marked 'work in progress'; the CLI exposes a BIOME_THREADS env var to control worker threads, implying multi-threaded file processing
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — explain: formatting claims 97% Prettier compatibility and ships `biome migrate prettier`, so it's close to drop-in for Prettier; linting is not drop-in for ESLint — different config format/rule engine, no ESLint plugin support, and `biome migrate eslint` only best-effort converts recognized rules

gotchas: Type-aware lint rules (project domain: noFloatingPromises, noUnresolvedImports, noImportCycles) are opt-in and materially slower — docs cite ~800ms to ~2s per 2,000 files when enabled, plus higher memory use.
No incremental/cached formatting: every `biome format`/`check` run reformats cold, unlike Prettier/dprint — confirmed in Biome's own benchmark notes.
Formatter hit a real perf cliff on large parenthesized object expressions in arrow functions, reported as 'dramatically slower' between 2.5.10 and 2.5.13 (GH #11747).
Dual-licensed MIT OR Apache-2.0 per Cargo.toml/package.json, though GitHub's repo-level license detection reports just Apache-2.0.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Biome over Oxlint when you need one tool for both formatting and linting plus LSP/editor support and a Prettier-config migrator; Oxlint's README claims ~2x faster linting than Biome and 50-100x vs ESLint but is lint-only with no formatter. Ruff is the closest analog outside JS (Rust linter+formatter replacing Flake8+Black) if you're evaluating the pattern rather than a JS-specific tool.
verified_claims_summary: The only public numbers are Nov 2022 hyperfine runs on a MacBook Pro 13-inch M1 (2020) comparing Biome's Rome-era predecessor against Prettier, parallel-prettier/xargs -P prettier, and dprint for formatting (~25x, ~20x, ~20x, and 1.5-2x faster respectively, single-threaded ~7x), and against ESLint for linting (~15x faster, rules both tools support, no type-aware rules, single-threaded ~4x), plus a separate M1 Max 10-core run cited for a '100x faster than Prettier' figure. No compiler flags, tool versions, or raw output are given, and the benchmark/ directory that produced these numbers was deleted from main in commit 8e4ada5 (2026-05-13).
status_note: Actively maintained (pushed 2026-09-24, 25.9k stars, not archived); dual MIT/Apache-2.0, published as compiled binaries for every major OS/arch, so it's safe to adopt for day-to-day formatting/linting today — just don't cite the 2022 speedup numbers as current without re-benchmarking.
